utterances.text: I apologise. He has a hard copy. It should be 6D716 on the screen for purposes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't realize he had the hard copy there. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did, in fact, any entity or formation entitled the MUP command exist within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, to your knowledge, in 1999 or any time? You can answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that such a command existed, and I never saw such a heading as this one. I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for P1613 to be called up, the only other document I know of that has the title MUP command, that's dated the 27th of August, 1999, for an action in Dobrodeljane. Can we have both. There we go. We have both the English and the Serb up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see this is an order dated the 27th of August, 1998 [sic], for an action in Dobrodeljane, labelled military secret. If we can look at the last page of the document, we see a stamp and signature that I think speaks for itself. My question relates to item number 7 on this page. With respect to item number 7, we see that the command is supposed to be operated from the IKM in the region of Djakovica sector through brigade commanders. Did you ever hear of any such organ within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia known as the IKM in the Djakovica sector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on, then. You were shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On just a more broader basis, have you never heard reference in any context, either army or police, to a forward command post in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were shown a document by Mr. Bakrac, 5D1418, a telegram that you sent to the MUP staff and a response telegram received.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at the first page of the same, I think it's the first page, I'll see in a second. I guess it's the second page of the exhibit, Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This second page of the exhibit which is the telegram back to you, does this document specify what particular person or individual at the MUP staff would have signed this telegram and sent it back to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does -- does this document, this telegram, evident who signed or prepared this telegram on behalf of the MUP staff and sent it to you? Is there an author identified in this document, an individual author?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise anyone from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question, I believe. Do you know of any other person being named in 1997 to replace Obrad Stevanovic as commander of all PJP units, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN ZIVALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness, Your Honour; although, I do have a request. In reviewing the transcript during the break, we believe that there was an issue on -- that the transcript didn't reflect everything that was said at paragraph -- pardon me, page 13, line 23, through page 14, line 6. I suggest that the audio track be reviewed, and that's probably the easiest way to deal with that issue, since it was a lengthy response. I think that would -- I would request that that be undertaken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We agree that that answer relates to a matter of some importance, and we shall, therefore, ask CLSS to review the B/C/S tape and to provide us with a formal translation of page 13, line 23 to page 14, line 6 of today's transcript. Mr. Zivaljevic, that completes your evidence here. Thank you for coming to The Hague to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our next witness, Your Honour, is Mr. Adamovic, who is being handled by my colleague, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll need help from the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to open that binder, the one that's in front of you. On the top, there is a statement. Could you please take a look at it. Are those your signatures on this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you gave to the Defence of Mr. Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today, if you were to be asked the same questions, would you give the same answers that you gave when we took this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Adamovic. Those are all the questions that we have for the time being; our Defence, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just kindly ask the Trial Chamber to have Mr. Adamovic's statement admitted into evidence as 6D1613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Adamovic. Actually, I have one single, very brief question for you. Do you remember the meeting that was held at the MUP staff on the 22nd of July, 1998, where you attended?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following: At that meeting, let me jog your memory. You remember the participants, Sreten Lukic and so on. I don't want to show you the document because we've shown it hundreds of times. It is P -- 6D798, the meeting at the MUP staff on the 22nd of July, 1998. It was displayed several times. Anyway, do you remember, at that meeting, did General Obrad or General Rodja mention the establishment of some kind of a Joint Command headed by a civilian? Was there any reference to that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I remember no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman, and I represent General Pavkovic in these proceedings. I have a few questions I want to ask you. I understand from your statement that you left Kosovo on the 29th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was like the fourth day after the bombing started, or the fifth day?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The fifth day probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I understand that was because you were wounded, is that -- am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you will recall - and I assume you have your statement there in front of you - but you recall, in your statement, you talk at length about the proposition that neither the MUP staff nor any MUP units were involved in planning anti-terrorist activities, that the planning was done by the Pristina Corps. That's your position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it your knowledge about that extends through the 29th, when you left, and not after; fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to imagine with you a hypothetical situation so we don't get bogged down or try not to get bogged down. I think your position is that MUP units would be provided with maps that were created by the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So a PJP unit, for instance, provided with a map that shows the ground upon which an action is going to take place and the location of various units involved in that, who provided the orders to the PJP for exactly what it was that they were to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No special orders were issued; only excerpts from maps were provided that had been drawn up by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I understand you are a -- you have attended the military academy, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know how the system of command and orders and things of that nature work in the military because of that training, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way, generally speaking, that I do know but at a lower level, because I was trained at a lower level as far as the military is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's kind of where we're going anyhow, so that's perfect. Would you agree with me that the hierarchy in the order process for carrying out an action in the military is kind of like this: That there is an order that is drafted by the commander of the corps, in this case we're talking about the Pristina Corps; then that order goes down to the brigades and the command of the brigade then draws an order which he sends out to his battle groups that are going to be involved in carrying out that action; and then the battle group commander drafts an order which he sends out to the battle group commanders that are going to be involved in that; and, finally, there is a map of that more detailed order along with a coded map. That's the process of putting together an operation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is probably the case as far as the army is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And no unit commander in the army, or I suggest to you in the MUP either or the PJP, would even think about carrying out an action of the complexity of the kind of actions we're talking about here just based on a map that somebody drew, would it? You just can't do it based on a map, can you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what I did; that is to say, that I received from the Pristina Corps excerpts of maps and such excerpts were sent to commanders. I assume that, in the field, they did encounter military commanders where they would discuss in greater detail the tasks that awaited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that the commanders of the MUP units would actually draft the orders necessary to carry out these operations? It couldn't have been done any other way, could it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot claim what it was that they did out in the field because I was in the staff in Pristina, and I did not go out into the field; that is to say, as I've already said, they received excerpts from orders. What they did with their subordinate officers, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see these maps that you claim were provided by the Pristina Corps, these excerpts?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did see them since I went to the Pristina Corps, and I took these excerpts and I submitted them to commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any of those maps in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I did, some.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to have you look at a map and ask you if this is maybe one of those ones you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 6D01619, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not at all interested in the action that this deals with. I'm just interested in whether this is the kind of map you're talking about. It is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were like this, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it -- I don't read Serbian all that well, but why don't you read for us that little block down there in the lower left-hand corner, and we'll get it translated. It starts with "odluka." I kind of know what that means. Just read it out loud so the translators can translate it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: "Decision of the commander for destroying DTS in the area of Kosmac, excerpt for" and I assume that this is "company of the PJP." If I can see this right, it seems to be "Prizren, coded map Drim." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After "izvod za" there, those characters are written there in Cyrillic, and I think it's the name of MUP detachment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, it's not a detachment; it's one company on this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Then underneath that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just on moment, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Lukic, has this been submitted for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, as a matter of fact, they have withdrawn this from their 65 ter request, but it's still sitting in e-court and I wanted to ask the witness about it. So it may be admitted as an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you will have to submit it for translation, if you wish to rely on it, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do that. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right underneath, then, the last line, read that last line for us, then, will you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: "Coded map, Drim."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is a map that's known in military circles as a code map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I see, that's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, even if it wasn't written there, I suggest you would know that because it has all these little circles on it with numbers in them. Do you see all those little circles with numbers all over that map?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those little circles with numbers are code numbers, so that when unit a reporting by radio from the field its location, it can report its location in relation to one of those numbers without disclosing to the enemy exactly where they are. That's all that's all about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, one can see that these code numbers are there for units to communicate, those that are in action, to find their way in the area, to communicate amongst themselves, and to report to one another on the problems, rather, that they may encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, well, I'm not going to ask you that question. I've changed my mind. Well, let me ask you this: Did you ever see any actual written orders crafted by the Pristina Corps directing any MUP units as to what they were supposed to do, an actual written order for a MUP unit, or did you just see the maps?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: During the preparations here, I did see some orders, certain orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those were orders that would be orders for a unit of the MUP to carry out that had been drafted, in your view, by the VJ, the Pristina Corps, or somebody?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At least in terms of what I saw, orders were made by the Pristina Corps only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, in as much as the MUP was never actually resubordinated to the VJ, I take it somebody in MUP was responsible for approving these orders that were drafted by the VJ. Somebody had to say, "Yes, I agree. I order this PJP unit to carry out this task." Somebody had to approve that since they were not obligated to carry out any VJ orders unless it was approved by somebody at command level in MUP. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it cannot be said that there was approval by the MUP because I was in contact with the representatives of the Pristina Corps. I took these excerpts from maps, and I would submit them to officers in the field. So there was no special approval in the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you are submitting those maps to commanders in the field, it must be you that is approving those orders and telling them to carry them out. Actually, you're ordering that they be carried out by giving those maps, didn't you? Even if you don't say the word "order," that's what you were doing. If you didn't think they ought to be doing it, you wouldn't give them the map, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it cannot be put that way, that I was issuing orders, because, indeed, I was not issuing orders. So the basis for police action was the plan that had been adopted for carrying out anti-terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if I'm a commander of a PJP unit and you hand me a map like this, who is it that's ordering me to carry out the instructions that might be contained on that map? I mean, how am I supposed to know what to do if somebody isn't telling me, "You are ordered by this organization to carry out this activity"? It just can't happen any other way, can it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, previously, I don't remember the exact date, but before actions would start, meetings would be held at the staff, and then the plan would be discussed for carrying out anti-terrorist actions; that is to say, the Army of Yugoslavia and the police. That was the basis for further action on the part of all officers who were already out in the field and who had been engaged for that, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that starts to make sense. So what you're saying is that these actions would be discussed before in the MUP staff; the MUP staff headed by General Lukic would approve the action; and then when you received the map that basically was permission for you to go ahead and pass it on down to the commander. So it really was a planning process that took place in the MUP staff, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object, Your Honour, because the question starts with, "so what you are saying is that," and the witness is not saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, in your own interests, this needs either to be broken down or left for the words of the witness to some extent. It's not clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- who would be involved in these discussions, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're very right about that, but he certainly said that meetings would be held at the staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and the plan would be discussed for carrying out anti-terrorist actions. So at least Mr. Lukic's objection is not well-founded, I don't think, in that regard, but I will ask it in a little bit different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These meetings at the MUP staff, who would be in attendance at these meetings where you would discuss these actions?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings were usually attended by commanders of detachments and chiefs of secretariats; most often, that is. I'm speaking in general terms about meetings that were held at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, of course, members of the staff would be there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And why would you have these meetings? What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the period that we're talking about. If we're talking about the period before the anti-terrorist actions started, there were -- well, I cannot tell you exactly whether there was one or two meetings --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I want to talk about the period where you say that orders and maps and things of that nature are being prepared by the Pristina Corps and passed along to you, and that you are handing maps to commanders. You just told us there were meetings where these things were discussed. You told us who was at the meetings. I want to know what you talked about. What did you talk about at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, meetings were not held for carrying out each and every anti-terrorist action. Meetings were held only at the beginning. If we're talking about the implementation of actions and a plan, before an action would start, there would be a meeting that would be attended by officers from the Pristina Corps. At that meeting, all the attendees would be familiarized with the plan for carrying out anti-terrorist actions and -- now, whether all of that happened on the same day or within one or two days. There would be a meeting with the commanders of the detachments and the chiefs of the SUPs where the assistant ministers, generals - that is to say, General Djordjevic and General Obrad Stevanovic - told the officers about the tasks that were to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many of those meetings do you think there were while you were there? Let's just take that little bit of time between the 22nd and the 29th, that week, how many meetings were there that week that you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to tell you how many. I know there was a meeting with representatives of the Pristina Corps, whether it was at that meeting or a day later. In any case, there was a meeting at which the generals acquainted the officers with the plan to carry out anti-terrorist actions. As far as I remember, in those few days, even the minister may have been there, once the actions commenced, of course. A lot of time has passed, and it is difficult for me to recall everything, especially the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We'll go back now to where we started this. You are a -- at the time, you were an officer in the MUP. You had subordinates under you, you had superiors above you, you had come up through a chain obviously, and you certainly wouldn't do anything unless you had gotten approval to do it from your superiors in. Some form. Now, from whom did you get approval to pass these maps to the units that were supposed to carry out an action? Who gave you approval to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Separate approvals were not needed. I was in contact with representatives of the Pristina Corps. I would take the map excerpts and distribute them to the officers in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who approved you doing that? Blanket approval, specific approval, I don't care which, what made it okay with your superiors for you to pass those maps along to your units? Who approved you doing that? I don't think that's a difficult question. Somebody told you it was okay for you to do that. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: To repeat yet again, special approval could not come from just anyone. I was appointed on behalf of the staff before the actions commenced to contact the Pristina Corps and to distribute it further on in the field what I get from them. Of course, the leader or the head of the staff knew about those actions being planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were appointed by who to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the leader of the staff who appointed me on behalf of the staff to have contacts with the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The leader of the staff was General Lukic; is that who we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it, if you're standing there - I just want to picture you standing there - you've been handed a map. Who handed it to you? Where did you get it from? Who brought it to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was in contact, for the most part, with Colonel Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: He was the officer with whom I had most frequent contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you would get this map then, it's been handed to you, I guess you would look at it, and I guess that you would make some determinations about it like what units you should pass it to, like whether or not the things depicted on it were possible for your units to carry out. I assume you would make some kind of judgements about it like that, for no other reason just for the protection of your own forces. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I made no decisions regarding that issue. I was a member of the staff who would go to the Pristina Corps and forward information on the units in the area or in the territory. The Pristina Corps knew of that. I didn't go into any analysis of the maps and excerpts. There was no need for me to do so. I was not authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were just basically a post office box. They would come stick the map in you, and somebody would come fish it out of you and walk away with it. You had absolutely no authority at all; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying it quite that way. I'm merely telling you what I was doing. I explained how I established contacts and what it was that I told Colonel Djakovic. The outlines of the maps would most frequently be done before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was your rank at this point? Were you a colonel or what were you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why didn't they just have a sergeant or somebody doing that? This wasn't something that required a high-paid, high-level officer since you had no -- you didn't even bother to look at the maps, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know why it was me who did that. It is obvious that people at lower levels could have performed the same duty that I did when it comes to these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So a courier, instead of bringing the map to you or General Djakovic, instead of bringing it to you, could have just sent it off to those units and skip you completely, but you were getting paid the big bucks as lieutenant-colonel. I don't understand what you were doing there, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to implementing the tasks, my role was an auxiliary one. I was on the sidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, did you know anything about the status of the field? When I say that, did you know, for instance, in a particular village how many KLA troops were believed to be stationed there? Did you know things like that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, not even those things. I wasn't included and I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, who would look at these maps and say, "Well, let's see, that PJP unit is being asked to attack a particular area, and there are a hundred of them and there are a thousand KLA there, that's ridiculous"? Who would look at a map and make a determination like that? Who from the MUP staff would make those kind of determinations before they would send their troops into a situation where they could all be killed, for instance? Didn't somebody exercise some kind of authority over this situation?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one made such assessments in the staff. It is obvious that the Pristina Corps had information on the forces in the area. I suppose, based on that information, they made maps; and the Army of Yugoslavia would be included, as well as the PJP, on the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's just get really practical about this. You say that you were handed a map without doing anything beyond having kind of a general authority to hand it over. You gave it to a unit, and let's just say, for instance, that that unit was completely wiped out, killed by KLA, the whole unit, because they were attacking a vastly superior force. Who in the MUP is responsible for that? Who takes the hit for that, because somebody's going to be in trouble for sending that unit against such a vast force. Who is that going to be? Who in the MUP chain of command gets in trouble for that? You?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, it would be the minister or the sector chief since they deployed the forces in the field. To repeat again, the staff did not participate in the planning and execution of anti-terrorist actions. It was done by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just don't understand why the minister of the interior would send a whole bunch of high-ranking police officers and create an organization in Kosovo called the MUP staff and then not give them any authority to do anything. How does that make any sense? It just seems like a huge waste of people and money and everything else. I mean, did somebody just tell you that you needed to come here and say those things, or was that the way it really was?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The real situation was the way I'm describing it. At the MUP staff, we had very few officers. In order to deal with such issues in a more serious manner, there should have been many more officers who would participate in these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that Kosovo with bombs falling on it is not a very good place to go for a rest, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to refer you to paragraph 31 of your statement. First of all, you begin with the language: "During my stay at the staff," which we've already established was about five days. You say that: "During my stay at the staff, the Pristina Corps planned all big operations." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: All actions that included both the army and the police were planned by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the words you used, I think in your statement, are "big operations," right? That's what I asked you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I use the word "bigger" actions. What I had in mind were the actions in which the army and police participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other side of that, I guess, is that the MUP planned smaller actions, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the MUP planned smaller actions if there was a need to do so. While the anti-terrorist actions were being executed, the plans were being made by the Pristina Corps. These were priorities, and those actions were the ones to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that only once now, but that's not my question. My question was: When you say that the big actions were planned by the Pristina Corps, the other side of that is the smaller operations must have been planned by the MUP. And that's just follows, doesn't it? It makes sense, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It does make sense; however, I'm telling you that while the anti-terrorist planned actions were being under way, including both the army and the police, they were focused on. If there were smaller anti-terrorist actions, if there is something happening in the territory of a given secretariat, and if the secretariat with its own forces could see the task through, they did. This doesn't require many members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to have you take a look in a minute at P1505. While we're waiting for that to come up, I want to ask you in -- during the time you were in Kosovo and even before that, Vlajko Stojiljkovic was the minister of the interior, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, it was Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Before him, there were other ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I take it that the minister of the interior has the authority to create an organization like the MUP staff and has the authority to determine what its tasks will be and what its authority will be, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It should be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it actually was like that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the documents I saw here, one wouldn't be able to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look where you may be talking about. The one we're getting ready to look at is P1505.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we look at it after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, are we there already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time flies when you're enjoying yourself, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when we were interrupted by the break, we were looking at an exhibit designated P1505, and I want you to look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll have to go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at paragraph 2 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There we go, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you see paragraph 2 there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're a professional policeman. What does that mean to you? If you had gotten such a document, what would that mean to you to read that? What does it tell you to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I would conclude that I was to go about the tasks set out in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Like planning, organizing, and managing the activities and use of the organizational units of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is not only to the those that are attached to you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: However, the reality looked differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We may get into that. That reply is not only to the units that are attached to your staff but those that have been sent, I guess, from Serbia to assist, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And all to do with suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then the second paragraph, as near as I can tell, says basically the same thing; to plan, organize, direct, and coordinate the activities of the police units in Kosovo in carrying out complex, big operations, security operations; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to interrupt at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the question, it says "police units." In the document, it says "organizational units," I think, in paragraph 2 of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can't assume that that's organizational units within the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but SUPs, OUPs, and things like that, but not PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I accept that. I wasn't trying to limit it, Your Honour. It's just a poor choice of words on my part, I guess, but I don't think I need to take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Lukic, that the PJP is not an organizational unit of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, but I think it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's, no doubt, a matter for submission in due course, in light of various rules and other regulations we have to consider. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, is the minister of the interior superior to the PJP?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The minister of internal affairs is superior to all members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we were looking at paragraph 3, and I think that you've read that. What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says that the head of the staff is answerable for the work of the staff on the security situation to the minister; and, of course, he's supposed to inform him on all security-related events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, the absolute number one person in charge of the police - and when I say "police," I mean all organizations of the Ministry of the Interior - the person absolutely number one in charge of all those organizations is the person who signed this document, Vlajko Stojiljkovic. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the minister heads the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would he -- why would he order these kinds of things that are contained in paragraph 2 and 3? Why would he sign a document with those two paragraphs in it if he didn't mean it? Was it just some kind of a game he was playing? Was he just kidding or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to comment what the minister had in mind. If we have a look at this, and if we compared that with the practice, it is obvious that these tasks are not good. Whether he was aware of it at the time or not, whether he knew what and how things would develop in Kosovo, I don't know. I really cannot comment on what the minister had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there, and so there's a lot of things I don't know; and you were there, and there's probably a lot of things you do know. Was there kind of a general sense that the minister was not competent and not able to do his job properly? Was that kind of what everybody was feeling about Stojiljkovic at that point and just kind of laughing at the stuff he was doing?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't say so, particularly since I never saw this document. I wasn't familiar with what is stated therein. However, it is clear that it does not correspond to the situation in the field, the facts that were in existence in the field and how things were being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do I understand that you think it's important to say that the document doesn't correspond to what was going on in the field, and you've now said it three times and you probably don't need to say it again, and maybe what you can do is concentrate on the questions I ask you. So, as far as you know, the minister was competent and able to do his job during this period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It should be correct. We know who he was appointed by. I cannot go into analysing the minister and his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I take it, if you had been the head of this staff that this decision is directed to, that you would have taken those two paragraphs seriously and would have treated them seriously, and attempted the best way you could, as a professional officer, to carry out the tasks set out there, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way; however, this document, now when it was written, was it the minister's idea to really have the staff do this, as written here? I really don't know that. But, obviously, in terms of what was happening in the field, as the situation grew more complex, as there was larger-scale terrorism, quite simply it was impossible for the staff to do all of this with the number of people that were there on the staff; that is to say, that this requires a large number of people to be involved in all of this, professional, well-trained, so that this could function and that this work could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that we know who he was appointed by, referring to Stojiljkovic. Who was he appointed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that goes into the sphere of politics. I think he was appointed by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. What do you mean by: "We all know who he was appointed by," please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're talking about the minister, as a reference was made to the minister, his qualities, and so on. I'm saying that the police does not decide who the minister is going to be. When Mr. Vlajko was in that position, not before that, not after that, it is only natural that the police has its own impressions about the minister, if I can put it that way; but we have no say, no one asks us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just out of the blue, you made this statement: "We know who he was appointed by ..." Now, I would like you to give me a frank answer as to what that refers to and who it refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that I had any special intentions when I said that. The questions persisted on the minister's qualities, whether he is capable of doing the job and so on and so forth. So then I said that we from the police quite simply do not take part in such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing that in mind that there was some dissatisfaction according to you with his performance, you seem to be pointing in the direction of an appointment by somebody that might explain that. So who was the somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't mean anyone specifically, anyone in particular. I'm saying that this belongs to the sphere of politics. As a professional, I tried to stay away from politics, as far away as possible. That's why I put it that way. When the office is set up, too, when the -- or rather, when a cabinet is being proposed by a prime minister designate, whatever, I don't even know how that goes. I try to be a professional and to leave politics aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You appear to be doing precisely the opposite by yourself introducing this reference which was not called for by anyone. So I ask you again: Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really did not mean anyone specifically. How consultations develop in the sphere of politics, I really don't know. It is possible that I misspoke, if I can put it that way, but the essence is what I've been saying so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder - again, you know, I wasn't there and you were so you know a lot more about this - I wonder if there was some kind of a culture that had grown up in the police ranks that basically called for ignoring anything that police ministers did, ministers of the interior did, that they could simply be ignored and you could just go about doing things the way you wanted to? Is that what happened, they just become figureheads with no power?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say that the police ever ignored orders they received from their leadership. The police acted in accordance with the law and the powers they had. When speaking of this particular matter, anti-terrorist actions, for us it was the decision of the state organs that was of significance; namely, that the police had to carry out certain tasks regardless of whether somebody liked that or not. That is the price to be paid by this professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go talk about something else now because we've kind of taken up too much time, I think. You're familiar with groups called RPOs, reserve police branches or stations, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of reserve police branches or stations, "odelenja."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, they existed during the time that you were active in Kosovo, did they not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that they were organized and armed by the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Not only by the police, they were armed by the army and police as far as I know; although, I was not involved with reserve police branches or stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who's Ljubinko Cvetic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubinko Cvetic, at that time, he was chief of the secretariat in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't want to do this, but I'm going to have to have you look at P1114. And I'll just tell you, without having to go to the last page, that this is a document from Ljubinko Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we can just go to page -- just as an example go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a document that talks about the creation of all of those RPOs in Kosovska Mitrovica secretariat. And if you look about halfway down that page - it's the bottom of the B/C/S that you're looking at - it talks about the numbers of rifles that have been delivered to various RPO members, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, then, if we look at P2804.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we need to go I think to the second page in the B/C/S. This is just the cover page we have there. Yeah, it's hard to read though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You should see a paragraph that begins with: "Organize defence of the villages with the newly formed reserve police stations, and with that aim in mind build defence fortifications ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that document is signed by General Lukic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then it says, I think: "For each RPO, make a dossier," maybe "containing security assessment of the threat for the RP O, the task of the RPO, a training plan, a defence plan, a communications plan, and ammunition replenishment plan, a control plan." Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look now at 6D808. This is dated 1 April 1999; and, of course, that's after you left Kosovo, but I'm just going to rely on your knowledge as a police officer, senior police officer, as to the meaning basically. The -- what we see at the top is it was delivered to the secretariats of the interior in all these locations; Pristina, Pec, Djakovica, Prizren, Urosevac, Gnjilane maybe, right, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that first paragraph interests me because it talks about the new situation caused by NATO bombardment, and it says: "It's necessary that you submit a daily summary of important incidents and events from 0600 hours to 0600 hours to the staff of the ministry of the Republic of Serbia for the autonomous province of Kosovo. Send it by fax by 0700 hours the next day." The question I have about that -- this is ordered by General Lukic. The question I have about that was: Why? To what purpose? Since the staff had no real control over anything, what difference did it make whether that was sent to them or not? Why would he order that? Why does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, even before that probably, and in that period, the staff submitted reports to the Ministry of the Interior about security-related incidents in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. What I know is that these reports were all brought together for the entire territory of the province, and they were submitted to the Ministry of the Interior. I think they were also submitted to the secretariats in Kosovo so that they would be aware of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at subparagraph, there's a list there starting with the number 1 as to what he wants included in this summary. If you look at number 3, he wants information about serious crimes committed. He wants to know the time, the place, the manner, the perpetrator, the victims, the result, the degree of the crime, murder, robbery, theft, looting, and rape, and the measures that were taken. Does that indicate to you that at that point, on the 1st of April, that General Lukic was aware that such crimes were, in fact, being committed and that he wanted a report on them?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It does not mean that he knows that crimes were committed. If I can put it this way, these are incidents that are of interest; and if they happened, they should be recorded and this kind of a compiled report should be sent to the ministry, as in the previous two points. So, if there are such crimes, of course, they are going to submit information; and if there are no crimes, then there is no submission of information. At least that is what this document seems to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess it was just drafting what he meant to say was if serious crimes were committed, rather than telling about the serious crimes committed, right? That's your analysis of it at least, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, something that is committed is one thing and suspicion that something was committed then you wouldn't write this way. This is information that preceded what happened in Kosovo, if I can put it that way. This belongs to the domain of reporting that is only natural on the part of all secretariats, regardless of the area involved, regardless of whether it's Kosovo or outside Kosovo; that is to say, such information is provided to the ministry. Prosecution is a different matter, but these are incidents in terms of whether they happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So maybe we can say he expected those kinds of things to be happening, so he wanted to know about them when they do; fair?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the wording is right, that it is expected to happen. That is police work. Everything that the police knows and everything that is noteworthy has to go through the system of reporting. Even in these situations, since these are serious crimes, these are rules of action which require urgent reporting on such matters. So that is what the -- what was valid in Kosovo and outside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So these things would have been reported to him even if he hadn't issued this document, because just normal police procedure would require that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way, but I assume that this is yet another reminder of such matters. I don't know how else to interpret this; that is to say that, this is what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On two or three occasions now, when I've asked you a question, you have said: "It can be put that way." I'm taking those answers to mean: Yes, that's a way to look at it; you're right. Is that what those answers mean, that I'm correct in that assertion?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am presenting one assertion; that is to say, that the members of the Ministry of the Interior always had to act in accordance with the law and bylaws that regulate certain rules of how members of the service should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They had to follow orders when they received them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: To carry out orders, yes, except for those that constitute a crime. Members of the service cannot and should not carry out such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not a crime to engage in planning activities, anti-terrorist activities, as Minister Stojiljkovic ordered, is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that question. Mr. Ackerman, we're going to have to strike some sort of balance in this cross-examination because I understand there are perhaps more extensive than normal requests. So can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I've gone at least a half-hour longer than I've expected this to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's had to do with the length of the answers and the sidetracks that the answers have created. I don't know what to do. I've got about six more documents I would like to discuss with him and some of them will be awfully fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. This is an important witness and, therefore, we're happy to trust your judgement, but we're showing signs at the moment of getting bogged down in something that wasn't really advancing our knowledge of matters very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've done that before, as you've observed, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1989. This is the minutes of a meeting of senior police officials in Kosovo-Metohija on the 4th of April, 1999, like ten days into the war. General Stevanovic is there; Major Lukic is there; the chiefs of all the secretariats are there; the PJP commanders are there, SAJ, RDB, JSO, the whole gang. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the RDB -- actually, just a moment, please. Yes, yes, I see it on there underneath the agenda -- no, no, no. Commander of the JSO RDB; not the chief of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move over to paragraph 2 in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on page 3 in the English. It's probably close to that in Serbian, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a paragraph entitled: "Forthcoming tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whoops. We have the Serbian now on the right-hand side, but we've lost the English. We've got the Serbian on both sides. There we go. Now we got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These are tasks that are being assigned apparently by General Lukic, head of the staff of the ministry. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, oh, one, two, three, four, five, six, it looks like the seventh bullet point, he says: "Take rigorous measures towards paramilitary units ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, then, if we go to the bottom, right before the Assistant Minister Stevanovic speaks, he again makes it clear that the secretariat chiefs and the unit commanders must report to the MUP staff. Now, I want you to look at the next page, I think it is in B/C/S and English, and we see Obrad Stevanovic, assistant minister, and his instructions. In the very last one, it says, to the heads of all these organizations that are working in the field and dealing with terrorists: "Conduct cooperation with the VJ through the commander on the ground and inform the staff of any problems." Now, the way I read that is the process of dealing with cooperation in activities with the army are to be worked out with the ground commander from the VJ and the ground commander from the MUP, just between themselves on the ground, rather than at some higher level; is that what that says? Does that make sense in that context?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: What is written is that cooperation with the army should be carried out through the commanders on the ground -- the commander on the ground. The commander of the army and the commander of the police, that is the reference that is made, that they should cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go quickly to 6D778. It's a one-page document. We should get through it rather quickly. You'll see that this is a document from General Lukic to all the secretariats and some separate police units, detachments 21st to 87th. In it, he speaks about an order that was entered on the 5th of April, to prevent civilians from leaving their places of residence and to ensure their safety and take measures to protect the population. He says it's come to his attention that some people are not obeying that order, as they should have been, and he makes it very clear that that order must be obeyed and that persons who failed to do so would be held accountable. Now, if there is a plan to expel the population from Albania, why would anybody sign and circulate such an order? It doesn't make sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: A plan to expel the Albanian population, as far as I know, did not exist. This pertains to the period during which I was not with the staff. Always, or frequently, at all meetings that were held, both secretariat chiefs, as well as detachment commanders, were told to act lawfully when implementing tasks, in particular to protect civilians in all situations. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move now quickly to 6D874. This one now we're up to the 6th of May. This is another document from General Lukic directed to the chiefs of all the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija. He says that because of the NATO aggression crimes and other unlawful acts have been committed in a new way in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, properties being unlawfully appropriated, things of that nature. Then, in a few paragraphs down, he says: "In order to disrupt and eliminate all adverse developments in the security situation and to ... prevent the perpetration of the most serious crimes and ... to arrest the perpetrators, particularly ... murders, rapes, and various types of ill-treatment, theft, aggravated theft, arson and ... damage to private property, it's necessary to" do certain things: Collect a bunch of information and establish cooperation with state security and the army, cooperation with public prosecutors ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is: This is the kind of an order to try to get control of and prevent and punish crime that commanders are required to do under the law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, as you said, this concerned crimes; however, I do not see that in this circular. What I see is that people are being reminded of their obligations in terms of their conduct when it comes to individuals who were committing illegal acts. What is requested is that people act lawfully and that people should be prosecuted if information is acquired that they had participated in the commission of certain crimes, irrespective of whether they were policemen or else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly my question. My question exactly is that. You know that the law requires a commander to take steps to prevent or punish crime, and that's just what General Lukic is doing here. It's what a commander is supposed to do, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Commander, or rather, not the commander, but the leader or the head of the staff did not have the authority to undertake specific measures against such individuals. If they were criminally liable, we know what should have happened and we know what the police was supposed to do. If there were disciplinary breaches, again it wasn't up to the commander -- excuse me, the head of the staff to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this is another one of those orders like that first one we looked at from Stojiljkovic, where it really wasn't serious, nobody needed to pay attention to it. Is that what you're saying? He had no power to issue the order, so people would just ignore him; is that your point?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't fully understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not even going to try to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is very simple. What is the point of this if the person sending it has got no authority to deal with or do anything about the information he gets? We're in a war with little time to spare, if any, and the suggestion is this is a pointless document. So what do you say was the point of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've said something of the sort already. The role of the staff, among its other roles, was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer the question. What's the point of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, that the secretariats are reminded of their obligations. I didn't carefully go through the whole document, so as to be able to say exactly what I think of it. If we look into it, it is requested that urgent measures be taken in terms of prosecuting crimes. All perpetrators should be prosecuted in case they violated the authority of the police and the laws pertaining to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to another document, 6D773, a very short document. Can you shed any light on what this document is, from who to who, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: One can see from the document that the MUP staff is sending it to the secretariat in Pec and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Then it says: "Send the civilians from," what's Djurdjevdan? Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't, I don't, since I wasn't in Kosovo then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Djurdjevdan operation, so there must have been some kind of operation, but it says maybe a code-name, you think?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. According to this, it was the name of an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, so, it is ordering that the civilians from that operation should be sent back to their places of residence and that they should undertake all security measures, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, one concludes that, after certain actions, civilians moved to safer areas. Once the actions were completed, as we can see, the intention was -- or rather, the tendency was to see the population back to their places of residence, to their homes, and that the police should undertake all security measures. This should mean that it shouldn't be allowed for some irresponsible individuals to be able to do something that would be contrary to the law and to the rules of conduct in any situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On whose authority would this have been sent? Who had the authority to issue this order in the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The intention was to retain the population in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the question is: Who had authority to send this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see -- actually, there is no signature, I've just noticed. The head of the staff should have been familiar with this dispatch that was sent -- rather, I don't really know whether he was informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's still not an answer to the question. Who in the MUP staff had or would have the authority to issue such a document? Who in the MUP staff could do this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we don't need you to start this evening, but how long are you likely to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Roughly two hours, Your Honour, but I will check one more time my questions and maybe I will cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there is certainly no point in repeating the areas that have already been dealt with. We would be grateful if you can look again at what's necessary in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, we need to bring today's proceedings to an end and adjourn until tomorrow. That means you need to come back here to continue your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Meanwhile, it's a strict rule that we have that you should have no communication of any kind with anyone at all about any aspect of the evidence in this case. So please bear that in mind. Please leave the courtroom now with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
